summary.value: This paper proposed the CO3, Contrasting concepts compose better, to improve muti-concept prompt fidelity in text-to-image diffusion models. Instead of re-training, the authors introduced a corrective sampling strategy, to steer away from regions where the joint prompt behavior overlaps strongly with any single concept in the prompt. Specifically, they analyze and show that composition through weighted sum of Tweedie-means in the Tweedie denoised space, offers a more general framework. Experiments on diverse multi-concept prompts demonstrate improvements in concept coverage, balance and robustness, with fewer dropped or distorted concepts compared to standard baselines and prior compositional works.

strengths.value:
1)	The paper is well-written, and the structure is well-organized. 
2)	The proposed CO3 is plug-and-play, model-agnostic, and gradient-free. And the results shows stronger semantic alignment to prompts. 
3)	Combing the strengths of correction-based approaches and composable diffusion seem reasonable and effective.

weaknesses.value:
1)	Some very latest and more relevant works are not compared, such as, Magnet (We Never Know How Text-to-Image Diffusion Models Work, Until We Learn How Vision-Language Models Function), TWEEDIEMIX ICLR 2025, ConceptWeaver, etc. 
2)	It is confusing that why using arbitrary weights in (10) (i.e., Liu et al. 200) does not lead to a valid Tweedie-mean. There seems a lack of theoretical analysis or empirical validation.
3)	How to connect the equation (12) to (13). On other words, why (13) is representing the samping from the unnormalized probability distribution in Eq. (12).
4)	More experiments are tested on two concept prompts. Can this model generalize to the scenario with the prompts of three or more concepts?

>__Q1. Some very latest and more relevant works are not compared, such as, Magnet (We Never Know How Text-to-Image Diffusion Models Work, Until We Learn How Vision-Language Models Function), TWEEDIEMIX ICLR 2025, ConceptWeaver, etc__

Thank you for pointing out these recent work. We have now added new results on Magnet and TweedieMix. We note that both TweedieMix and ConceptWeaver operate in the concept-customization regime: they require a fine-tuned LoRA (or customized embedding) for each concept involved. A fair, apples-to-apples comparison on our benchmarks and baselines would therefore require (i) collecting or generating additional training images for every concept, and (ii) fine-tuning a separate LoRA model for each of the hundreds of concepts that appear across our prompts - both computationally infeasible and fundamentally different from our setting. CO3, in contrast, is a training-free, model-agnostic inference method that does not rely on concept-specific customization. To still provide insight, we adapt TweedieMix’s sampling strategy only (without its customization stage) and report these results below.  We see that, CO3 still outperforms both Tweediemix and Magnet almost across all categories (except for Magnet’s strong performance in Objects-Objects in BLIP-VQA metric).

comment.value:
>__Q2. It is confusing that why using arbitrary weights in (10) (i.e., Liu et al. 200) does not lead to a valid Tweedie-mean. There seems a lack of theoretical analysis or empirical validation.__

Thank you for raising this question and we apologize if our explanation was not clear. 

In our setting, for a fixed linear–Gaussian forward process, the Tweedie mean at step $t$ under classifier-free guidance (CFG) has the form

$\hat{x}\_{tweedie}(x\_t, c)
= (x\_t - \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}\_t}\,\epsilon\_\theta^{\mathrm{cfg}}(x\_t, c, t)) / \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}\_t}.$



This can be rewritten as

$$
\hat{x}_0(x_t, c) = a_t x_t + b_t(c),
$$

where $a\_t = 1 / \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}\_t}$
 is fixed by the noise schedule and does not depend on the conditioning $c$. The term $\epsilon_\theta^{cfg}\$ is the usual linear combination of conditional and unconditional noise predictions.

Now consider the linear combination of scores used in Eq. (11) of Liu et al.[1]. If we use it in the expression at the top, for $\tilde{x}_{tweedie}$ to be the Tweedie mean of some conditional joint distribution $p(x_t \mid c_1, c_2,..,c_k)$ under the same forward process, its dependence on $x_t$ must again take the form $a\_t x\_t + b\_t(\cdot)$ with the same coefficient $a\_t$. This forces the normalization constraint

$$
\sum_i w_i = 1.
$$

Thus, when mixing scores from different conditional distributions, the above condition need to be satisfied for $\tilde{x}\_{tweedie}$ to correspond to any coherent joint conditional model. Eq. (11) of Liu et al. allows arbitrary weights, which in general violate these constraints. In such cases, the result is simply a heuristic linear combination of scores, and the resultant Tweedie mean doesn't correspond to any well-defined distribution under the given forward process. This is what we meant by “does not lead to a valid Tweedie mean.”

By contrast, CO3 composes Tweedie-means from different conditional distributions. Lemma 1 shows that these weights have to satisfy the same unit-sum condition as above for the resultant composed Tweedie-mean to be a valid one.  CO3 maintains this condition and  this preserves the update on the Tweedie manifold of the underlying sampler. 

We will augment the derivation in Appendix A.4 with this explanation.

 

[1] Liu, Nan, Shuang Li, Yilun Du, Antonio Torralba, and Joshua B. Tenenbaum. "Compositional visual generation with composable diffusion models." In European conference on computer vision, pp. 423-439. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2022.

comment.value:
>__Q3. How to connect the equation (12) to (13). On other words, why (13) is representing the sampling from the unnormalized probability distribution in Eq. (12).__

 

Thank you for raising this question. 

Eq. (12) defines the CO3 corrector distribution at timestep $t$ by down-weighting regions where the joint distribution $p_t(x \mid C) $ overlaps with individual concept distributions $p_t(x \mid c_i) $. It introduces the unnormalized density:

$$
\log \tilde{p}\_t(x \mid C)
= w\_0 \log p\_t(x \mid C) - \sum\_{i=1}^K w\_i \log p\_t(x \mid c\_i).
$$

The resulting score is a weighted linear combination of per-prompt scores.

By Tweedie’s formula, for any conditioning $c$, the Tweedie mean satisfies:

$$
\hat{x}\_{tweedie}(x\_t, c)
= x\_t + \sigma\_t \nabla\_{x\_t} \log p\_t(x\_t \mid c),
$$

where $\sigma_t$ depends only on the noise schedule. Therefore, any linear combination of scores corresponds to the same linear combination of Tweedie means (up to the shared $x_t$ term).

Eq. (13) implements this by composing the joint and per-concept Tweedie means with the same weights. Plugging this into the DDIM update yields a probability-flow sampler (Eq. 5–6), and iterating at fixed $t$ samples from $\tilde{p}_t(x \mid C)$ (see Algorithms 2 & 3). 

Finally, we emphasize that composing in Tweedie-mean space is more general than working directly in score space. As proven in the paper (Lemma 1), any sampler whose update can be expressed in terms of $\hat{x}\_{tweedie}$ can adopt the same CO3 composition rule. This provides a unified view that recovers standard compositional-score methods as a special case.

>__Q4. More experiments are tested on two concept prompts. Can this model generalize to the scenario with the prompts of three or more concepts?__

Yes, CO3 generalizes to 3 or more concepts. In addition to our main evaluations on Attend-Excite prompts (which contain relatively simple two-concept compositions), we have included new experiments on the Complex category of T2I-CompBench as well as the Concat, Relation, and Complex categories of RareBench. These subsets were chosen because they specifically stress multi-concept interactions, attribute entanglement, and rare or low-support combinations. Compared to the simpler Attend-Excite cases, these categories contain more challenging, high-entropy compositions and therefore serve as stronger tests of compositional fidelity.  As pointed out by R2F [1],  BLIP-VQA can be unreliable in the rare-concepts regime. We follow the RareBench recommendation and report metrics that better reflect human judgement. Specifically, we report ImageReward and human evaluation from 11 participants.

summary.value: The authors proposed a method for better prompt-aligned multi-concept image generation. Specifically, existing models often neglect or mix multiple concepts in a single generation scenario. The proposed method tends to squeeze the distribution, hindering the generation process from walking through some problematic regions. The probability normalization approach is designed for this purpose.

strengths.value:

2. The distribution correction idea is theoretically intuitive and good.

>__Q2a. In the ablation study, the corrector’s contribution is somehow questioned: a) What is the performance of SDXL+Corrector (w/o Re-sampler)?__

We update the ablation table with the additional entry of SDXL+Corrector.  

Including the Corrector alone already improves performance in categories where attributes must attach to specific objects. This is most clearly visible in Rows 4–5 of the ablation table: prompts of the form “a [attribute1][object1] and [attribute2][object2]” show large gains, because early-timestep dominance (one object absorbing both attributes) is the failure mode that the Corrector resolves.

>__Q2.b In all 6 metrics, it has gains only in 3 metrics, out of 6. The other 3 are either the same or even worse__

The Corrector specifically targets concept–attribute misalignment, so it is understandable that its performance is not pronounced in categories such as animals-animals (i.e., prompts of the form *“a [animal1] and a [animal2]”*). Thus, improvements appear strongest in the categories that reflect attribute fidelity and multi-object separation.  Importantly, the average performance of *SDXL + Corrector + weight-modulation (last row)* is very close to the *SDXL + Resampling + Corrector + weight-modulation (4th row)*  which indicates the Corrector is powerful even without Resampling. But the full improvement is achieved when the Corrector is applied after the Resampling steps, so that weight-modulation together with the Corrector mitigates concept dominance and improves concept-attribute alignment.

>__Q3. In Table 3, it has the worst speed performance, and even the metrics are not great compared with ToMe__

Although CO3 takes more time compared to ToMe with 50 time-steps, it takes much less memory. CO3 is light-weight and it’s peak memory requirement is only slightly above the base SDXL model. ToMe is gradient based methods and has significant memory requirement. 
Also we want to emphasize that CO3 is model-agnostic and can be applied to any diffusion-based model. Compared to that, ToMe is model-architecture dependent where its attribute binding approach works by manipulating the internal attention activations of the base-model.

We have added new figures to Appendix A.7.9. 

 

>__Q5. There is no limitation section.__

We apologize for not including the limitation section before. We are updating the paper with such as section, mainly discussing the following three items:
- In obeying the prompt, CO3 seems to be suppressing the richness of the background. We would like to offer control on background generation without sacrificing the prompt obedience.  
- CO3 lacks a mechanism to adaptively select/adjust the number of Resampling or Corrector steps.  
- Similar to other baselines, CO3 has room for improvement in concept-attribute alignment. 

 

>__Q6. Low  image quality in Figure 5. Limited color diversity in qualitative results in Figure 3.__

Thanks for raising an interesting observation. We investigated it further. What initially appears as reduced visual richness in a few simple cases (e.g., Fig. 5) is in fact a consistent manifestation of *CO3’s stronger prompt obedience*. CO3 tends to strongly obey the concepts specified in the prompt; when the background is not specified it is conservative with hallucinating the background. However if the background is explicitly specified, CO3 brings the same degree of richness and quality to both the foreground and the background. 
We have added a discussion and new figures in Appendix A.7.8, that enriches the "low quality" images in Figure 5 based on explicitly specified backgrounds.

summary.value: This paper tackles the problem of multi-concept compositional generation in text-to-image diffusion models. The authors hypothesize such models struggle with compositional generation because the learned joint distribution for composite prompts overlaps significantly with individual concept distributions, leading to dominance by a single concept. To address this, they propose CO3, a plug-and-play corrective sampling method that suppresses individual concepts by re-weighting Tweedie means of each concept, rather than directly re-weighting in the noise (or score) space. Experiments on SD1.5, SDXL, and Pixart-$\Sigma$ show improved prompt alignment and concept coexistence.

strengths.value:
1. CO3 requires no retraining or gradient computation and can be applied to any diffusion model. This makes it broadly applicable and practical.
2. The paper provides an intuitive theoretical explanation showing that directly performing weighted averaging of scores does not guarantee a valid Tweedie mean or consistent classifier-free guidance formulation; by instead re-weighting in the Tweedie-denoised space, CO3 ensures mathematical validity.
3. Novelty. While not the first to explore Tweedie-denoised space reweighting for concept composition [1], CO3 offers a clear theoretical formulation and a practical two-stage approach, early resampling followed by later correction, that together provide consistent empirical improvements and strong interpretability.

[1] Kwon & Ye, TweedieMix: Improving Multi-Concept Fusion for Diffusion-based Image/Video Generation, ICLR 2025.

weaknesses.value:
My main concern lies in the evaluation, particularly regarding benchmark coverage and baseline selection.

1. The evaluated prompts are relatively limited, focusing mainly on compositions involving animals and objects. Incorporating commonly used benchmarks such as T2I-CompBench, which include more diverse attribute and object combinations, would strengthen the empirical validation.
2. A relevant baseline is missing [1]. In addition, comparisons with recent **LLM-guided generation methods** [2, 3, 4] would be beneficial to quantitatively assess the relative performance and effectiveness of CO3 in enhancing compositional fidelity. If the proposed method is orthogonal to LLM-guided approaches, it would be particularly valuable to demonstrate how CO3 complements them when combined.
3. Including comparisons with recent **state-of-the-art text-to-image models**, such as **Stable Diffusion 3.5** or **Flux**, would improve the paper’s relevance and help readers better understand the practical significance of the proposed method.

[1] Yu et al., Improving Compositional Generation with Diffusion Models Using Lift Scores, ICML 2025.

[2] Yang et al., Mastering text-to-image diffusion: Recaptioning, planning, and generating with multimodal llms, ICML 2024.

[3] Lian et al., LLM-grounded Diffusion: Enhancing Prompt Understanding of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Large Language Models, TMLR 2024.

[4] Hu et al., ELLA: Equip Diffusion Models with LLM for Enhanced Semantic Alignment, arXiv preprint.

summary.value: The paper addresses the problem of multi-concept prompt fidelity in text-to-image diffusion models. The authors propose CO3, a lightweight, re-training-free corrective sampling strategy that adjusts inference to maintain balanced representation among multiple concepts. By analyzing the instability of existing compositional guidance, the method identifies stable composition-weight regions and steers sampling toward them. CO3 integrates seamlessly with classifier-free guidance and demonstrates improved concept balance, coverage, and robustness across diverse prompts compared with prior compositional baselines.

strengths.value:
1. Correction‑based compositional guidance with theoretical grounding and broad evidence.
- The method unifies ideas from correction‑based approaches and composable diffusion into a single re‑training‑free sampling framework, and provides a reasonable theoretical justification for composition‑weight choices and stability regions. The paper offers extensive quantitative and qualitative comparisons that demonstrate improvements in multi‑concept fidelity while remaining compatible with standard classifier‑free guidance.

weaknesses.value:
1. Comparison on multi‑concepts is incomplete.
- The paper focuses on improving multi‑concept prompt fidelity, especially when one concept is rare or easily dominated by another. A direct theoretical and empirical comparison with R2F [1], ideally on RareBench, would clarify relative strengths on the rare‑concept regime where fidelity typically degrades most.

2. Model coverage could be broadened beyond SDXL.
- To strengthen the claim of generality, evaluations on additional recent open‑source text‑to‑image diffusion models, for example FLUX, would make the comparisons more persuasive and reduce the risk that gains are specific to one backbone.


Reference

[1] Park et al., Rare‑to‑Frequent (R2F): Unlocking Compositional Generation Power of Diffusion Models on Rare Concepts with LLM Guidance.

questions.value:
1. Compatibility with low‑step and high‑order solvers.
- Main experiments use SDXL with a 50‑step DDIM sampler. Can CO3 be applied effectively with high‑order solvers such as DPM++ at around 10 steps, and with distilled text‑to‑image models that operate at 4 steps or fewer? Any guidance on tuning composition weights in these low‑step regimes would be helpful.

2. Human evaluation.
- ImageReward and BLIP‑VQA are useful proxy metrics, but has a human evaluation been conducted to assess concept presence and balance under multi‑concept prompts? If not, a small user study could substantiate the claimed improvements in perceived fidelity.

> __Q1. Comparison with R2F, ideally on RareBench, would clarify relative strengths on the rare‑concept regime where fidelity typically degrades most.__  
 
Thank you for the suggestion. We have added a direct comparison with R2F on RareBench (multi-concept categories). As pointed out by R2F,  BLIP-VQA can be unreliable in the rare-concept regime due to strong frequency priors, hence we follow the RareBench recommendation and report metrics that better reflect human judgement. Specifically, we use ImageReward and human evaluation.  

Results are reported in the Table below. Across most categories, CO3 achieves higher rare-concept fidelity than both the base model, R2F, and our most competitive baselines from Table 1 in the main paper.

We note that CO3 is not designed specifically for rare-concept scenarios — it is a general compositional sampling correction that does not rely on rarity-aware priors or LLM-based prompt augmentation. Yet, we were pleasantly surprised that CO3 matches or exceeds R2F on RareBench, despite R2F being tailored for rare-concept generation. We believe this indicates that the early-alignment phase of CO3, which mitigates concept dominance and encourages sampling from ”pure” modes, is naturally beneficial for rare-concept generation as well. Although CO3 is not explicitly designed for rarity, its ability to reduce dominance effects in the training distribution appears to translate into stronger fidelity on rare concepts.

 

| Method         | ImageReward (concat) | ImageReward (relation) | ImageReward (complex) | Human Eval (concat) | Human Eval (relation) | Human Eval (complex) |
|----------------|----------------------|------------------------|-----------------------|--------------------|----------------------|---------------------|
| SDXL   | 0.1018            | 0.3607              | 1.1907            | 0.5416             | 0.5016               | 0.6283              |
| ToME   | -0.2041            | -0.0632              | 1.0203              | 0.4500             | 0.4983               | 0.4866             |
| R2F    | -0.0162              | 0.3620               | 1.1542                | 0.4300             | 0.5200               | 0.5366             |
| Co3    | 0.1610             | 0.2588              | 1.2211            | 0.6167             | 0.6200               | 0.6116             |

 



**Theoretical comparison with R2F:**  

Thank you for raising this point. We agree that clarifying the theoretical relationship between R2F and CO3 helps contextualize their respective strengths. Both methods aim to address failures in multi-concept diffusion generation, but they do so from different theoretical perspectives and intervention mechanisms.  

-  Where the approaches *agree:*  
Both R2F and CO3 identify that compositional errors arise during inference due to concept dominance, mode overlap, or mixing in the sampling trajectories of common and less-frequent concepts. Both are training-free interventions that seek to improve semantic alignment without modifying model weights. R2F mitigates dominance for rare concepts by enriching the conditioning path with frequent conceptual anchors, while CO3 mitigates dominance more generally by correcting the score trajectory to avoid mixed-mode drift.  

- Where the approaches are *different:*  
R2F is tailored for rare-concept compositions: its theory assumes that rare concepts lack training support and uses LLM-identified frequent sub-concepts to guide the denoising path from “rare → frequent”. We think CO3 addresses a broader failure mode that occurs even with common concepts: the diffusion sampler may drift into entangled modes where one concept overwhelms others. CO3 directly intervenes in the sampling path through early score alignment and dominance-reduction, without relying on LLM guidance or rarity-specific priors. Conceptually, R2F modifies the conditioning distribution, while CO3 modifies the sampling distribution.  

- In conclusion:  
Since CO3 operates directly at the sampler level and is agnostic to whether a concept is rare or frequent, it generalizes naturally across compositional tasks. This is evident in the RareBench experiments above, where  CO3 outperforms R2F on the majority of rare-concept categories, despite not being designed for rarity. This suggests that CO3’s dominance-mitigation mechanism—steering sampling toward cleaner, less-entangled modes—is inherently effective even in the rare-concept regime. We view CO3 and R2F as complementary: combining conditioning-level rare-concept anchoring with sampler-level dominance correction is a promising direction for future work.

Thank you for the detailed and thoughtful revision. The added RareBench comparison, expanded theoretical discussion with R2F, low-step solver experiments, PixArt evaluation, and the new human-evaluation study substantially strengthen the paper and address the main concerns I previously raised. These additions make the contribution notably clearer and more convincing. For completeness, I would still like to highlight a couple of remaining limitations.

- Extremely low-step regimes are not covered: while the new 10–20-step results are helpful, the behavior under highly distilled 1–4-step samplers remains an open question.

Even with these points, the revisions meaningfully improve the submission, and the key issues regarding rare-concept evaluation, solver compatibility, and human studies have been satisfactorily addressed. I will adjust my score accordingly.

summary.value: This paper proposes CO3, a gradient-free compositional guidance method for multi-concept text-to-image generation that addresses concept missing/fading issues by modifying the sampling distribution to avoid mode overlap. The method unifies correction and composable diffusion approaches through a Tweedie-mean composition framework. Initial reviews were mixed & borderline with concerns about missing baselines and limited evaluation scope. The authors provided an exceptionally comprehensive rebuttal with many new experiments addressing almost all concerns, including comparisons with recent methods, evaluations on additional benchmarks, tests on new architectures, human evaluations, and extensive ablations. Overall, I think the paper proposes a simple yet effective training-free sampling method for image generative models.
